title: Cocaine dependence: “Side effects” and syndrome formation within 1–12 months after first cocaine use

claims.statement: In US household surveys from 2002 to 2016 (National Surveys on Drug Use and Health), among people who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview, an estimated 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) of those who had used only powder, and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) of those who had gone on to crack, met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were interviewed; the estimates are summaries of seven two-year survey pairs, based on 3,488 and 275 powder-only and powder-then-crack initiates in all (9 to 96 per year-pair in the second group). Of 21 dependence-related problems asked about, the most frequent in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine (45.4%, 43.1% to 47.9%, against 58.3%, 53.0% to 64.2%) and the least frequent was continuing to use despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine (1.9% against 2.8%, the difference not significant); most of the other problems were more common in the group who had gone on to crack, with at least one exception and one item whose estimate the paper does not plot. The two groups are not comparable exposures: the comparison is unadjusted, the survey asks about cocaine in any form rather than which form caused a problem, and reaching crack within the same 12 months takes time and continued use, so time since first use, which is not reported for either group, and amount used may differ. The paper's authors give three readings of the difference without choosing between them: people who go on to crack may be more susceptible from the outset; some may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking may raise the risk. The figures rest on self-reported diagnosis in a household and group-quarters survey (people in institutions are outside the sampling frame), without characteristics reported for either group, and the item wording sits in supplements that were not available. The 22% is not shown to be the same as the roughly 30% reported for newly started heroin use in a separate study: no test is reported and the interval stops at 29.4%. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Chandra & Anthony (2020), meta-analysis summaries of seven two-year survey pairs: dependence within 1–12 months of first use 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) in powder-only initiates and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) in powder-then-crack initiates (the paper's Conclusions print 20% for the second). Year-pair estimates 2.9% to 7.0% and 10.3% to 30.0%, the widest interval running from 9.2% to 64.5%. Problem items: wanting or trying to cut down or stop 45.4% (43.1% to 47.9%) against 58.3% (53.0% to 64.2%), difference p < 0.05; continuing to use despite physical problems 1.9% (1.6% to 2.4%) against 2.8% (1.6% to 5.2%), p > 0.05. The study card's reading of the figure: powder-only estimates below 10% for 17 of the 20 plotted items, powder-then-crack estimates 15% or more for 14; one item about equal in the two groups and one (about 36% against 28%) higher in the powder-only group. No adjusted estimate, no absolute difference with an interval and no per-month risk are given.
